transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-29
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Liu (Redwood SE), Sarah Patel (CTO, Pacifica Health), David Nguyen (ML Eng), Priya Rao (Head of Product), Liam O'Reilly (Infra), Maya Chen (Data Lead)

Summary (auto):
- POC scoping focused on cost modelling / unit economics for Pacifica's clinical summarization workload.
- Discussed workload sizing (avg token lengths, QPS, concurrency), batching/caching knobs, expected per-token cost, potential dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, and a 4-week POC timeline.
- Next steps: Redwood to send cost model spreadsheet, run sandbox benchmarks, Pacifica to share sample prompts and budget constraints.

Topics: cost model, batching, KV cache, quantization, POC timeline, success criteria, benchmarks

Transcript body:
[00:00] Elena (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Elena, AE on this one. With me is Marcus Liu, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Sarah (Pacifica): Good, thanks. Quick note, we've got a hard budget for the pilot so we'll need to tune the scope around that.
[00:12] Marcus (Redwood): Totally understood. Today we want to align on success criteria, expected workload, and then walk through a cost model and what knobs we can tune — batching, caching, quantization — that kind of thing.
[00:24] David (Pacifica): Sounds good. For context, our main workload is clinical note summarization: average prompt length ~120 tokens, average generated summary ~280 tokens, we estimate 6-8 QPS steady and peaks up to 35 QPS during end-of-day batch ingestion.
[00:42] Marcus: Great, that helps. Do you have an idea of concurrency and burst tolerance? Is 95th percentile latency target strict?
[00:48] Sarah: We'll target p95 < 300ms initially, but ideal is <200ms. If that means cost goes up we need to see the numbers.
[00:56] Elena: Got it. As a quick orientation: Redwood offers Hosted API and Dedicated capacity. For POC we typically run in our sandbox hosted infra but can spin up a small dedicated pool for apples-to-apples latency testing. There's also Private for VPC/on-prem but that adds time.
[01:14] Liam (Pacifica): Private is interesting for compliance but for the POC we're fine with hosted, as long as data is isolated and logs are handled — we can discuss paper later.
[01:22] Marcus: Noted. On cost assumptions, we use per-token pricing for generation + embedding units etc. For summarization the bulk is generation tokens. Two important levers: batching (increases throughput, reduces per-token cost but adds latency) and KV/prefix caching (saves repeated encoder tokens, big wins if prompts share prefixes).
[01:40] Maya (Pacifica): We do have a lot of repeated boilerplate in prompts, so caching could matter. How big are the savings typically?
[01:46] Marcus: Depends on repetition. If you have 40-60% overlap in prefixes between calls the per-token CPU/GPU work can drop substantially, maybe 20-40% cost improvement in practice. But that requires keeping KV cache warm and some memory on the instance.
[02:02] David: What about quantization—we're using open models mainly. If you do 8-bit quantized runtimes what is the accuracy/regression risk?
[02:09] Marcus: We recommend per-model profiling. 8-bit quantization often gives 2-5% quality delta on some tasks but many summarization tasks are tolerant. We'll flag any regressions via eval sets. For POC we can test fp16 vs int8 and report rouge/clinical fidelity metrics.
[02:24] Elena: Let's go through a quick back-of-envelope cost example so we have a baseline. If your avg request is 400 tokens total (prompt+response) and you do 6 QPS sustained, that's ~1.44M tokens per hour, ~34.6M tokens per day. Multiply by your target days in POC. But key is per-token unit price — for hosted it might be $0.0003/token for certain models (this is illustrative), for dedicated the unit cost to you changes with instance amortization.
[03:00] Sarah: That seems high — can you break down per-million tokens or per-1k tokens?
[03:05] Marcus: Sure. Example: at $0.0003 per token that equates to $300 per million tokens. If 34.6M tokens per day that's ~10.4k per day — again illustrative. But with batching and caching we can often reduce that by 25-40% for this type of workload.
[03:26] Priya (Pacifica): Our pilot budget is about $10k for the month—this is across infra and Redwood fees. How should we size the scope to stay within that?
[03:35] Elena: For a constrained $10k pilot, we recommend running targeted benchmarks: pick 3 workload slices (low, mid, end-of-day burst) and run 10k requests per slice to produce reliable p50/p95 and token counts. That should be doable in sandbox with careful throttling; we'll help with the harness.
[03:53] Marcus: We'll also provide a cost-model spreadsheet where we plug in your QPS, avg token lengths, batching parameters (batch size/latency target) and caching hit rates, and it outputs estimated monthly spend under hosted vs dedicated assumptions.
[04:07] David: Great — can you show the knobs? Like, what batch sizes are realistic for sub-200ms p95?
[04:13] Marcus: For small LLMs (e.g., 7-13B) you can run batch sizes 2-8 with little latency impact; for 70B models batching bigger helps throughput but latency increases. A general pattern: to meet p95 <200ms you'll likely cap batch sizes smaller or use more instances with lower occupancy. For p95 <300ms you have more room to batch and benefit.
[04:33] Sarah: We're leaning toward a smaller model family for cost reasons but want high fidelity in clinical summaries — tradeoff acknowledgement.
[04:40] Marcus: Right — another lever is quantized model variants specifically profiled by Redwood. We can suggest a few candidate models with verified perf/quality profiles.
[04:48] Priya: On success criteria, here's what matters: 1) p95 latency <300ms (goal <200ms), 2) summary quality within X% of our current human baseline (we'll define an eval set), 3) total pilot spend < $10k, and 4) integration effort < 2 engineer-weeks.
[05:03] Elena: Love that — clear and measurable. We'll capture those as the POC acceptance criteria.
[05:08] Marcus: For benchmarks we propose the following schedule: Week 1: data ingest and env setup, Week 2: baseline runs (fp16 hosted), Week 3: experiment with batching/caching and int8 runs, Week 4: optimize and handover + quality/regression checks. That aligns with a 4-week POC.
[05:25] Maya: If we see a quality regression after quantization, will you fall back automatically to higher-precision model?
[05:30] Marcus: We can set up a canary/fallback policy in the test harness so that if rouge/clincal-fidelity drops below threshold we revert to fp16. For production we also support runtime routing so critical calls go to higher-tier capacity.
[05:44] David: About benchmarks — how many samples to be statistically meaningful?
[05:48] Marcus: For perf p95 you want tens of thousands of requests, but for the POC we recommend 10k per slice as Elena suggested. For quality evals, 500-1k seeds is typically sufficient to surface major regressions.
[06:02] Sarah: Any additional hidden costs? Storage, logs, higher retention for audit?
[06:06] Elena: Storage and long-term trace retention are add-ons. Audit logs and heightened retention for compliance will add to cost; we'll list those in the spreadsheet and tag them as optional.
[06:16] Liam: For the hosted sandbox, what security controls are available? We need SSO, access logs, KMS integration ideally.
[06:22] Marcus: Sandbox supports SSO and RBAC; for KMS and dedicated key controls we typically do Dedicated or Private. We'll include the security docs pack.
[06:31] Priya: Can you run a small pilot on Dedicated just to compare latency numbers?
[06:35] Elena: Yes, we can spin a small dedicated pool for a short window for apples-to-apples. It affects cost and lead time (a couple days to provision) but it's doable as part of the POC.
[06:45] David: On the spreadsheet, will you show amortized dedicated costs? i.e., instance cost / expected token throughput?
[06:50] Marcus: Exactly. We'll show per-token amortized compute cost based on expected utilization, plus network and storage. We'll also show sensitivity: low-util vs high-util.
[06:58] Sarah: What's a realistic utilization target to make Dedicated cost-effective?
[07:02] Marcus: Generally >40-50% sustained utilization makes Dedicated attractive. If your usage is sporadic with big bursts, Hosted with smart routing and burst will often be cheaper.
[07:12] Priya: For the POC acceptance we'll want the spreadsheet to output monthly run-rate and also the POC-specific spend.
[07:18] Elena: We'll do both: line items for the POC run and then monthly run-rate scenarios.
[07:24] Maya: Can Redwood show examples from other healthcare customers (anonymized) where caching reduced cost?
[07:29] Elena: Yes, we have anonymized case studies and we'll include a 1-pager.
[07:33] David: One more technical detail: what's your KV cache TTL assumptions? We worry about memory pressure if TTLs are long.
[07:39] Marcus: TTLs are configurable; typical POC values are session-length (minutes) or per-shard. We'll help tune cache eviction policies. Memory depends on model size and KV entries; we'll estimate during profiling.
[07:53] Elena: Ok let's walk through a concrete sample cost calc — I'll speak through a simplified spreadsheet row. Assume 6 QPS steady, avg 400 tokens per request, 86.4M tokens/day — wait that's if 6 QPS * 3600 * 24 * 400? Let me re-calc —
[08:12] Marcus: Quick math check — 6 QPS * 3600 = 21,600 requests per hour, times 400 tokens = 8.64M tokens per hour, times 24 = 207.36M tokens/day. So we should make sure to clarify whether 6 QPS is per region or per workload.
[08:29] Elena: Good catch — thanks Marcus — that's a big delta. David, you earlier said 6-8 QPS but was that continuous or average over business hours?
[08:36] David: Sorry, that's during business hours — steady for ~10 hours per day. At night it's lower — maybe 0.5 QPS.
[08:42] Elena: Perfect. So let's model 10 hours at 6 QPS and 14 hours at 0.5 QPS — that gives a much lower total tokens/day. We'll capture that traffic profile in the sheet.
[08:52] Priya: Can we put a hard cap on POC spend? We want to avoid surprises.
[08:56] Elena: Absolutely. We'll set up budget alerts and caps for the sandbox run; for hosted usage we can enforce limits.
[09:02] Sarah: On timeline, we'll aim for start of POC week of 2027-01-04. Is that feasible?
[09:07] Marcus: Yes — if we get sample data and your acceptance criteria formalized by 2027-01-05 we can kick off. Provisioning dedicated nodes (if requested) may slip a couple days.
[09:17] David: Who will run the benchmark scripts — Redwood or us?
[09:20] Marcus: We can run them and give you the harness to re-run locally. We'll also provide guidance on metrics and monitoring.
[09:27] Maya: For quality metrics, we'll provide a labeled set of 600 clinical notes for rouge and clinicians to spot check. Is that sufficient?
[09:33] Marcus: Yes, 600 is a good start. We'll run regression checks across quantized and fp16 variants.
[09:39] Elena: Ok I'm going to summarize the agreed scope and next steps.
[09:42] Elena: 1) Redwood to send cost-model spreadsheet and recommended model list (by 2027-01-04). 2) Pacifica to share anonymized dataset and traffic profile (by 2027-01-05). 3) Redwood to provision sandbox and schedule baseline runs (Marcus by 2027-01-06). 4) Run 10k requests per workload slice and 600 quality evals in Week 2. 5) Week 3 experiment with batch/caching/quantization. 6) Week 4 final tuning and handover.
[10:08] Sarah: That aligns. Also please include the security docs (SOC2, dataflow, KMS options) in the pack.
[10:14] Elena: Will do.
[10:15] Priya: One last thing — for acceptance we want a short-run cost projection and the monthly projected run-rate under both hosted and dedicated scenarios.
[10:22] Marcus: We'll include both and sensitivity ranges for cache hit rate and batch size.
[10:26] Elena: Anything else from team?
[10:28] David: No, that's it from me.
[10:30] Sarah: Thanks everyone.
[10:31] Elena: Thanks — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and scheduling invites.
[10:35] (call ends)
